title: Meridian Bank Named a 2025 Baltimore Top Workplace by The Baltimore Sun
summary: The post Meridian Bank Named a 2025 Baltimore Top Workplace by The Baltimore Sun appeared first on Meridian Bank Investor Relations .
body_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE Contact: Christopher J. Annas 484.568.5001 CAnnas@meridianbanker.com Malvern, Pa. (December 12, 2025) – Meridian Bank, the wholly owned subsidiary of Meridian Corporation (Nasdaq: MRBK) has been named a Baltimore Top Workplace by The Baltimore Sun in its December 7 edition. Ranked ninth among midsize companies, Meridian is also the highest-ranking financial institution. The Top Workplaces program recognized Meridian for scoring well above other commercial banks in three key categories: pay (17% higher than benchmark), interdepartmental cooperation (16% higher) and execution (16% higher). Meridian also earned special recognition for ranking in the top 5% of its benchmark in four key culture areas: supportive managers, innovation, cross-team cooperation, and work-life balance. “Coming from another bank, joining the Meridian team has been extremely rewarding. What really sets Meridian apart—and why being named a Top Workplace means so much—is the personal support and sincere appreciation I receive for my contributions. It’s empowering to work for a company that values its people,” said Sunmeet Sawhney, VP, Residential Branch Manager. Only 38 companies made this year’s list, and the full list of winners can be found on The Baltimore Sun’s website or in its December 7 issue. The data was gathered through an anonymous survey of more than 215 Meridian Bank employees. Energage LLC partnered with The Baltimore Sun to administer the survey, which measured employee experiences, culture drivers and component themes within the organization including alignment, execution and connection. About Meridian Corporation Meridian Bank, the wholly owned subsidiary of Meridian Corporation (Nasdaq: MRBK), serves Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland and Florida through a network of bank branches, mortgage and wealth management offices. Offering a full suite of financial products and services, Meridian specializes in business and industrial lending, retail and commercial real estate lending, electronic payments and wealth management solutions, along with a menu of high-yield depository products, all supported by robust online and mobile access. For additional information, visit www.meridianbanker.com . Member FDIC. Equal Housing Lender.

body_text: By late 2025, most HR teams are no longer debating whether artificial intelligence belongs in people operations. It’s already there. The same is true for skills frameworks, hybrid work policies, and employee listening tools. What’s missing isn’t adoption. It’s consistency. Inside many organizations, AI screens candidates in one function but not another. Skills taxonomies exist in theory, while hiring managers still recruit by job title. Hybrid work rules vary by leader, not by role. Pay transparency requirements exist on paper, while compensation structures remain difficult to explain. None of this is theoretical. It’s the day-to-day reality HR leaders describe privately and increasingly, report publicly. Heading into 2026, the pressure on HR is less about choosing new priorities and more about making existing ones hold together. Boards want fewer pilots and clearer results. Employees want predictable rules. Legal teams want to know which tools touch employment decisions and why. That combination creates a narrow window. HR teams can either keep adding layers (new policies, new platforms, new statements of intent) or start fixing the gaps between them. This article focuses on the second path. What follows are the HR trends that matter in 2026 because they show up in operating reviews, compliance discussions, and attrition data. The Pressures Forcing HR Decisions in 2026 HR leaders heading into 2026 aren’t reacting to a single trend. They’re responding to a stack of pressures that compound each other and leave little room for delay. The first is AI moving from experimentation into daily workflow . Recruiting teams rely on automated screening. HR operations use algorithms to flag turnover risk. Learning platforms recommend skills paths without human review. Once these tools touch hiring, pay, or performance, they stop being “technology choices” and start becoming governance issues. Legal teams know it. Employees feel it. HR owns it. Next comes the skills problem , which most organizations still haven’t solved. Job architectures lag behind how work actually gets done. Teams need narrower, faster-to-deploy capabilities, while hiring systems still revolve around static roles. The result is friction everywhere: slower hiring, limited internal mobility, and managers who can’t find the skills they already pay for. Then there’s workforce fragmentation . Full-time employees no longer make up the entire operating workforce, even in conservative industries. Contractors, project-based specialists, outsourced teams, and embedded vendors now sit inside core workflows. Add automation to that mix and accountability blurs quickly. HR policies, built for a single employee population, struggle to stretch across this reality. At the same time, cost pressure hasn’t eased . Many organizations entered 2025 after layoffs, hiring freezes, or compensation resets. That context matters. HR is expected to protect engagement and retention while controlling spend, simplifying tech stacks, and justifying every headcount request with more rigor than before. Finally, there’s trust: quiet, fragile, and easy to damage. Employees pay closer attention to how decisions get made, not just what gets announced. Inconsistent flexibility rules, unexplained pay ranges, or opaque AI use erode credibility fast. Once trust slips, policy enforcement becomes harder and attrition easier. None of these pressures operate in isolation. Together, they explain why 2026 feels less like a planning year and more like a reckoning. HR teams can’t afford to treat AI, skills, work models, and culture as separate workstreams anymore. The trends that follow reflect that reality. They aren’t predictions. They’re responses to pressure that’s already in the system. Trend 1: AI Governance in People Decisions Becomes Standard Practice Context By 2026, artificial intelligence plays a role in many HR processes, particularly in recruiting, workforce planning, learning, and compensation. In most organizations, these tools were introduced incrementally, often by different teams and for different purposes, rather than through a single, coordinated strategy. As a result, AI use in HR is often distributed across systems, vendors, and workflows, with varying levels of documentation and oversight. Why governance is becoming necessary As AI systems increasingly influence employment-related outcomes, organizations face growing expectations to understand and explain how those systems operate. This applies most clearly in areas such as: Candidate screening and ranking Performance assessment and risk flagging Pay recommendations and equity analysis Skills and career path suggestions Once automated tools contribute to these decisions, they become part of the formal employment process. That shift changes how organizations need to manage them. What’s changing inside organizations In response, HR teams are moving away from informal oversight toward more structured governance. This does not usually take the form of broad policy statements. Instead, it involves practical controls, including: Maintaining an inventory of AI-enabled HR tools and use cases Clarifying ownership for each system and decision point Defining when human review is required Ensuring managers understand the limits and assumptions of system outputs These steps allow organizations to explain decisions more consistently and respond to internal or external questions with greater clarity. Implications for HR in 2026 AI governance is becoming a routine responsibility for HR, rather than a specialized or experimental one. As systems mature and scrutiny increases, the ability to trace how people decisions are made, and who is accountable for them, will matter as much as the tools themselves. This trend also sets up a broader reassessment of how work is defined. As organizations review decision logic more closely, many discover that traditional job structures no longer match how skills are applied in practice. That disconnect underlies the next major trend. Trend 2: Skills Replace Jobs as the Primary Way Work Gets Organized Context Many organizations enter 2026 with job architectures that no longer reflect how work is done. Roles bundle together tasks that change frequently, rely on outdated assumptions about career progression, or mask where critical skills actually sit. At the same time, business needs have become more variable. Teams assemble for specific outcomes, dissolve, and re-form. New tools reduce some tasks while increasing demand for others. In that environment, static job descriptions struggle to keep up. This gap has pushed skills from a secondary HR concept into a structural one. What’s changing Rather than treating jobs as fixed units, organizations increasingly break work into skills and capabilities. Hiring, internal mobility, and workforce planning then orient around those components instead of titles. This shows up in several ways: Job requirements narrow, focusing on essential skills rather than broad experience lists Internal talent marketplaces match people to short-term projects based on skills Learning investments target specific capability gaps tied to business priorities Career paths move laterally as often as they move upward The goal is not to eliminate jobs, but to reduce how much they dictate access to opportunity. Why this matters now Traditional job-based models create friction in fast-moving environments. They slow hiring, limit internal mobility, and make it harder to redeploy talent when priorities change. Skills-based approaches offer more flexibility, but they also surface problems that job structures often hide: Skills data is incomplete or inconsistent Managers struggle to assess skills objectively Employees lack visibility into which skills actually lead to growth Addressing these issues requires more than adding a skills taxonomy to an HR system. It requires changes in how organizations evaluate performance, design roles, and reward contribution. How organizations are responding HR teams taking this seriously focus less on perfect frameworks and more on practical use cases. Common starting points include: Identifying skills critical to a small set of priority roles or functions Using skills data to support internal moves before external hiring Aligning learning programs directly to those skills, not generic development plans Over time, these efforts begin to inform job architecture, compensation bands, and workforce planning decisions. Implications for HR in 2026 As skills take on greater importance, HR becomes responsible for maintaining a clearer picture of workforce capability. This shifts HR’s role from managing roles to managing capacity. It also changes how fairness and opportunity get evaluated. When access to projects, promotions, or pay depends on skills, organizations need confidence in how those skills are defined and assessed. This focus on skills feeds directly into the next trend. As work becomes more modular, the workforce itself becomes more mixed, employees, contractors, and external specialists working side by side. Trend 3: Workforce Fragmentation Forces a Broader View of Workforce Planning Context By 2026, the “workforce” in many organizations no longer refers only to employees on payroll. Core business work increasingly involves contractors, freelancers, outsourced teams, consultants, and technology-enabled services working alongside full-time staff. This mix didn’t appear overnight. It grew gradually, often driven by cost control, speed, or access to specialized skills. What’s new is how central these non-employee workers have become to day-to-day operations. What’s changing Workforce planning has traditionally focused on headcount, roles, and succession within the employee population. That approach leaves gaps when a significant portion of work happens outside that boundary. Organizations are now seeing: Critical projects staffed partly or entirely by external workers Teams that change composition frequently based on demand Functions where institutional knowledge sits with vendors or long-term contractors Automation taking on discrete tasks previously handled by junior roles As these patterns expand, planning based only on employees provides an incomplete picture of capacity and risk. Why this matters now Fragmentation complicates accountability, compliance, and continuity. Different worker types operate under different rules for access, performance management, data security, and termination. When responsibilities blur, so do ownership and oversight. It also affects cost visibility. Labor spend spreads across HR budgets, procurement, and operating expenses, making it harder to assess total workforce investment or compare options consistently. For HR, the challenge is less about managing every worker directly and more about ensuring the system makes sense as a whole. How organizations are responding HR teams are beginning to adopt a broader “total workforce” perspective. This does not mean collapsing all worker types into a single model. Instead, it involves coordination across functions. Common steps include: Mapping which work is performed by employees versus external workers Clarifying decision rights for hiring, onboarding, and offboarding across worker categories Aligning policies around access, security, and performance expectations Working with procurement and finance to improve visibility into labor costs These efforts help reduce operational gaps without forcing uniform treatment where it doesn’t fit. Implications for HR in 2026 As workforce composition grows more complex, HR’s role expands beyond traditional employment management. HR increasingly acts as a connector, aligning people strategy, procurement practices, and risk management around how work gets done. This trend also raises questions about fairness, development, and engagement. When external workers handle meaningful work but remain outside career and learning systems, organizations must decide where boundaries sit and why. The next trend addresses another tension shaping these decisions: pressure to control costs while maintaining engagement and performance. Trend 4: Cost Pressure Reshapes Employee Experience and Engagement Context Most organizations entering 2026 are doing so after several years of cost control. Layoffs, hiring freezes, delayed backfills, and tighter compensation cycles have affected how work gets done across functions. At the same time, expectations around employee experience have not reset downward. Employees still expect clarity, flexibility, fair pay, and manageable workloads, even as organizations operate with leaner structures. This creates a structural tension HR teams are already navigating. What’s changing Employee experience is no longer defined primarily by new programs or benefits. Instead, it is increasingly shaped by operational decisions tied to cost. This shows up in several ways: Roles expand as teams absorb work from unfilled positions Managers oversee larger spans of control Internal mobility is encouraged as a cost alternative to external hiring Learning budgets concentrate on business-critical skills rather than broad offerings In this environment, engagement depends less on what organizations add and more on how work is distributed and supported. Why this matters now Research from multiple HR advisory firms points to a clear pattern: engagement declines fastest when employees experience sustained workload imbalance without transparency or explanation. Cost control measures that lack context often feel arbitrary at the team level. Employees may accept limits on compensation or headcount, but they respond poorly when expectations rise without corresponding support or clarity. For HR, this shifts the challenge. The question is no longer how to “improve engagement” in the abstract, but how to help leaders manage capacity, prioritize work, and communicate trade-offs credibly. How organizations are responding Organizations taking a more deliberate approach focus on redesigning experience around constraints rather than trying to offset them. Common practices include: Setting clearer priorities to reduce low-value work Adjusting performance expectations to match available capacity Using internal mobility to fill gaps before approving new roles Giving managers better data on workload, attrition risk, and span of control These actions do not eliminate cost pressure, but they reduce the confusion and frustration that often accompany it. Implications for HR in 2026 Employee experience in 2026 is increasingly tied to how well organizations manage scarcity. HR’s role shifts toward helping leaders make trade-offs visible and consistent, rather than masking constraints with additional initiatives. This trend also intersects with earlier ones. Skills-based staffing, workforce fragmentation, and AI-enabled productivity all influence how cost pressure plays out at the employee level. The next trend focuses on one of the most visible expressions of that tension: how and where work gets done. Trend 5: Hybrid Work Settles Into Differentiated, Role-Based Models Context By 2026, most organizations are no longer debating whether hybrid work exists. The debate has narrowed to how it operates and who gets flexibility. Large employers have spent several years testing broad return-to-office mandates, looser hybrid guidelines, and manager-led discretion. The results are mixed. Uniform policies rarely align with how work actually happens across roles, while ad hoc flexibility creates inconsistency and employee resentment. What’s emerging instead is a more segmented approach. What’s changing Hybrid work is shifting away from one-size-fits-all rules toward models based on role requirements and team dependencies. Common patterns include: Certain roles designated as location-dependent due to collaboration, equipment, or client needs Other roles evaluated primarily on output, with fewer presence expectations Team-based norms replacing company-wide attendance targets Office time defined by purpose (planning, coordination, onboarding) rather than routine work This does not eliminate office presence. It narrows the rationale for it. Why this matters now Research consistently shows that dissatisfaction with hybrid work stems less from the number of in-office days and more from perceived unfairness and unpredictability . When similar roles operate under different rules, or when managers quietly override stated policies, trust erodes. Employees may comply, but engagement and retention suffer. At the same time, organizations have practical constraints, Real estate commitments, client expectations, regulatory requirements, that prevent fully flexible models. HR sits between these competing pressures. How organizations are responding HR teams are increasingly formalizing role-based flexibility rather than relying on informal norms. This includes: Defining location expectations as part of role design Documenting the business reasons behind those expectations Reducing manager discretion where it creates inconsistency Training leaders to explain flexibility decisions clearly and consistently The goal is not maximum flexibility, but understandable flexibility. Implications for HR in 2026 Hybrid work in 2026 becomes less about ideology and more about work design. HR’s role shifts from defending policies to helping leaders align presence with purpose and communicate those decisions credibly. This approach also intersects with workforce planning and skills strategies. As organizations clarify where work can happen, they widen or narrow talent pools accordingly. The next trend follows from this logic. As flexibility, cost pressure, and workload converge, employee well-being moves from a cultural topic to a business one. Trend 6: Pay Transparency Forces Compensation Architecture Cleanup Context By 2026, pay transparency is no longer limited to a handful of jurisdictions or early adopters. A mix of regulation, market pressure, and employee expectations has pushed compensation practices into clearer view. Many organizations responded initially by publishing salary ranges or adding compliance language to job postings. That addressed the surface requirement. It did not resolve the underlying issue: in many companies, pay structures are difficult to explain even internally. Transparency exposes those weaknesses quickly. What’s changing As salary information becomes easier to access, inconsistencies that once stayed internal now create friction with candidates and employees alike. Common fault lines include: Job levels that bundle dissimilar roles under the same pay band Wide salary ranges with no shared understanding of progression Pay decisions influenced by historical negotiation rather than role requirements Managers asked to explain ranges they didn’t help design In this environment, transparency does not create inequity, but it makes existing inequity visible. Why this matters now Research and employer reporting show that dissatisfaction around pay often stems less from the absolute number and more from confusion about how pay works. When employees cannot see how skills, performance, and experience connect to compensation, trust erodes. Questions escalate to HR. Managers struggle to answer them consistently. Recruiting slows as candidates challenge ranges early in the process. For HR, the cost shows up in time, credibility, and retention risk. How organizations are responding Rather than treating transparency as a disclosure problem, many HR teams are addressing it as a design problem. Key steps include: Reworking job architecture to clarify role scope and progression Narrowing pay bands and defining movement within them Documenting compensation philosophy in plain language Training managers to discuss pay decisions with confidence and consistency These efforts often require uncomfortable cleanup, correcting legacy decisions, adjusting titles, or standardizing exceptions that were never meant to scale. Implications for HR in 2026 Pay transparency in 2026 pushes HR toward greater discipline in compensation design. The emphasis shifts from calculation to explanation. HR teams that invest early in clear structures reduce downstream friction: fewer escalations, faster hiring conversations, and more credible pay discussions. Those that delay face ongoing pressure to justify decisions retroactively. This trend also ties back to earlier ones. As skills play a larger role in hiring and mobility, compensation systems must reflect that logic clearly, or risk undermining it. The next trend looks at a related pressure point: how much strain sits on managers as expectations rise across pay, performance, and flexibility. Trend 7: HR–IT Interdependence Becomes Structural Context By 2026, most HR priorities rely on technology decisions HR does not fully control. Artificial intelligence in people decisions, pay transparency, skills data, workforce analytics, and hybrid work infrastructure all depend on systems typically owned or governed by IT. For years, HR and IT worked alongside each other. In practice, responsibilities often stayed separate: HR defined needs, IT implemented tools. That boundary is no longer holding. What’s changing People data and technology are now tightly connected to risk, compliance, and business outcomes. As a result, HR and IT roles increasingly overlap. This shows up in several areas: AI tools that require data governance, security reviews, and audit trails Identity and access systems tied to onboarding, offboarding, and contingent labor Analytics platforms combining HR, finance, and operational data Vendor ecosystems that span HR, payroll, learning, and enterprise systems Decisions in one function increasingly affect the other, whether planned or not. Why this matters now Research and employer reporting point to a consistent pattern: when HR and IT operate independently, gaps emerge quickly. Examples include: AI tools approved without clarity on data sources or model limits Inconsistent access controls for employees and non-employees Duplicate or conflicting data across systems Delays when regulatory or audit questions arise These issues rarely stem from poor intent. They stem from unclear ownership and mismatched priorities. As scrutiny increases around AI use, data privacy, and employment decisions, organizations need clearer lines of accountability across both functions. How organizations are responding Rather than redefining reporting lines, many organizations are formalizing shared responsibility. Common approaches include: Joint HR–IT governance for people systems and AI use cases Shared roadmaps for HR technology, data, and analytics Clear escalation paths for risk, compliance, and data quality issues Agreed standards for vendor selection and system integration In these models, HR retains authority over people policy and outcomes, while IT ensures systems meet security, scalability, and compliance requirements. Implications for HR in 2026 HR–IT interdependence becomes an operating condition, not a project. HR leaders need enough technical literacy to ask the right questions, while IT leaders need enough context to understand people risks. Organizations that manage this partnership well reduce friction across multiple trends already discussed: AI governance, pay transparency, workforce fragmentation, and hybrid work. Those that do not often find themselves reacting to issues after systems are already in place. This dynamic also affects leadership capacity. As systems grow more complex, more responsibility lands with frontline and mid-level managers. That pressure defines the next trend. Where This Leaves HR Heading Into 2026 The HR trends shaping 2026 are not new ideas arriving all at once. They are the result of several years of decisions accumulating across systems, policies, and ways of working. Artificial intelligence in people decisions, skills-based models, workforce fragmentation, pay transparency, and hybrid work did not emerge in isolation. They intersect, and that intersection is where most complexity now sits. For HR leaders, the task ahead is less about choosing priorities and more about aligning them. AI use requires clearer governance. Skills strategies depend on credible job and pay structures. Hybrid work exposes gaps in role design and manager capability. Cost pressure forces trade-offs that must be explained, not obscured. What stands out across research and employer practice is a shift in emphasis. HR work in 2026 centers less on launching initiatives and more on maintaining coherence—between systems, expectations, and decisions. That coherence is what employees, leaders, regulators, and boards increasingly look for. This also reframes the role of HR itself. The function is no longer evaluated only on programs delivered or policies written, but on whether people decisions hold up when questioned. Can they be explained clearly? Are they applied consistently? Do they reflect how work actually gets done? Organizations that address these questions early reduce friction across hiring, retention, performance, and compliance. Those that delay often find themselves responding piecemeal, adjusting one issue at a time without resolving the underlying structure. 2026 does not require HR to reinvent its purpose. It requires discipline, clarity, and tighter integration across areas that were once managed separately. The trends outlined here point less to what’s next, and more to what needs to be brought into focus. Frequently Asked Questions About HR Trends in 2026 What are the most important HR trends for 2026? The most important HR trends for 2026 include AI governance in people decisions, skills-based workforce models, workforce fragmentation, pay transparency, role-based hybrid work, and tighter HR–IT collaboration. These trends reflect a shift from experimentation to operational consistency across HR systems and policies. How is AI affecting HR and people decisions in 2026? By 2026, AI directly influences recruiting, performance management, pay recommendations, learning, and workforce analytics. While often framed as “decision support,” these systems shape outcomes early in the process. This increases the need for AI governance, clear ownership, human review, and documentation within HR. What does skills-based HR actually mean? Skills-based HR focuses on capabilities rather than job titles alone. In 2026, many organizations use skills data to guide hiring, internal mobility, learning investments, and workforce planning. Jobs still exist, but skills increasingly determine access to opportunities, projects, and advancement. Why is pay transparency a major HR issue in 2026? Pay transparency exposes weaknesses in compensation structures that were previously hidden. Wide salary ranges, unclear leveling, and inconsistent pay decisions become harder to explain once salary information is public. The challenge for HR is less about disclosure and more about building compensation systems that are easy to understand and defend. How does workforce fragmentation change HR strategy? Workforce fragmentation means core work is increasingly performed by a mix of employees, contractors, external partners, and automated systems. HR strategy in 2026 expands beyond headcount planning to include coordination with procurement, IT, and legal around access, accountability, cost visibility, and risk. Is hybrid work still evolving in 2026? Yes, but the focus has changed. Hybrid work in 2026 is less about blanket policies and more about role-based expectations. Organizations increasingly define where work needs to happen based on role requirements rather than company-wide mandates, reducing inconsistency and employee frustration.

title: 10 top project management apps for growing teams in 2026

What are project management apps? Project management apps are software platforms that help teams plan, track, and deliver work across an organization. They go far beyond personal checklists or simple tracking sheets. Where a personal planner helps one person stay organized, a project management app coordinates entire project lifecycles — from initial scoping and capacity planning through execution, reporting, and retrospectives. At their core, these platforms provide 4 capabilities: Planning (timelines, milestones, dependencies) Tracking (progress, budgets, resources) Collaboration (shared workspaces, real-time updates, file sharing) Reporting (dashboards, analytics, status summaries). The best project management apps weave all 4 together so teams spend less time switching between apps and more time doing meaningful work. What challenges do project management apps solve? Growing without a centralized system creates compounding problems that get harder to fix the longer they persist. Here are the 4 challenges that send most organizations searching for a project management app in the first place. Recognizing which affect your team is the fastest path to choosing a platform that solves them. Scattered communication: Decisions get buried in email threads, chat channels, and meeting notes. When critical information lives in 5 places, nobody trusts any single source, and teams waste hours tracking down answers. Resource blind spots: Without real-time visibility into who’s overloaded and who has capacity, managers either burn out their top performers or leave budget on the table. Neither outcome scales. Manual status chasing: Hours disappear each week compiling updates across spreadsheets, slide decks, and one-on-one check-ins. When you’re asking “what’s the status?” more than “what’s the strategy?”, your process needs an upgrade. Strategy-execution disconnect: Leadership sets quarterly goals, but teams lose sight of them in the daily grind. Without a direct line between high-level objectives and individual workflows, organizations drift. What are the main benefits of project management apps? When the right platform is in place, teams stop working around their systems and start working through them. Here are the outcomes organizations can expect. Cross-functional visibility: Everyone from leadership to individual contributors sees the same real-time picture of what’s happening, what’s at risk, and what’s on track. Automated coordination: Workflow automation eliminates repetitive handoffs, status updates, and notifications, freeing teams to focus on work that requires human judgment. Faster decision-making: Dashboards and reporting surface insights without manual compilation. Leaders get answers in seconds, not days. Scalable operations: Processes that work for 10 people hold up for 10,000. How do the top project management apps compare on ease of use, integrations, and scalability? The ones built for growth let you add teams, departments, and workflows without rebuilding your foundation. Overall, the earlier an organization adopts a structured approach, the smoother every subsequent phase of growth becomes. Which teams benefit from project management apps? Is project management software only for project managers? Not even close. The most successful implementations span entire organizations. PMO and operations: Portfolio visibility, resource planning , governance frameworks, and cross-departmental alignment all live in one workspace. Marketing: Campaign coordination, creative approvals, content calendars, and launch timelines stay connected from brief to delivery. Engineering: Sprint planning , backlog management, release tracking, and bug triage follow structured, repeatable processes. HR and finance: Onboarding workflows, budget tracking, compliance processes, and audit trails benefit from the same automation and visibility. Enterprise-grade security: SOC 2/3, ISO, HIPAA eligibility, and FedRAMP “In Process” status meet stringent compliance requirements. Pricing Personal: Free for 1-2 users Starter: $10.99/user/month (billed annually) Advanced: $24.99/user/month (billed annually) Enterprise and Enterprise+: Custom pricing Considerations As teams scale, some users report a learning curve and occasional usability friction with advanced features . Paid plans require a minimum of 2 seats, which may affect solopreneurs or very small teams. 3. ClickUp For teams tired of toggling between windows, ClickUp offers a consolidated workspace that brings project management, docs, and chat under one roof. It targets cross-functional groups that want to reduce app sprawl, with 15+ views and extensive customization options for organizing work at every level. ClickUp’s Connected Search spans external apps like Google Drive and GitHub, and 100+ automation templates handle repetitive coordination. The mobile app supports most core functions for on-the-go management. However, AI features require a separate $5/user/month subscription on top of the base plan. Best for : Organizations aiming to unify their tech stack, from workflow tracking to document creation and team messaging , in a single interface . Key features Flexible visualization: Over 15 views including Gantt, Kanban, and workload management adapt to how different teams prefer to work. Native financial tracking: Built-in time tracking with roll-up reporting and billing integrations help teams manage budgets alongside projects. Connected Search: Search across external apps like Google Drive and GitHub without leaving the workspace. Pricing Free Forever: $0 (unlimited workflows, 60 MB storage) Unlimited: $7/user/month (billed annually) Business: $12/user/month (billed annually) Enterprise: Custom pricing AI add-on: $5/user/month Considerations The sheer volume of features can result in a steep learning curve for new users. Large workspaces may experience performance slowdowns, and extensive customization options require strong governance to prevent confusion. 4. Trello Visual thinkers often gravitate toward Trello , which popularized the digital Kanban board. By focusing on drag-and-drop simplicity, it lowers the barrier to entry for structured project management. Used by millions globally, Trello remains a go-to for teams that need a familiar, low-friction way to collaborate. Butler automation provides 200+ no-code recipes for handling repetitive actions, and workspace views offer cross-board rollups for program-level visibility. The mobile app is well-regarded for quick updates on the go. Best for : Small teams and visual thinkers who want lightweight, Kanban-style project tracking with minimal setup and fast onboarding . Key features Intuitive board views: Board, Timeline, Calendar, Table, Dashboard, and Map views let teams see work from multiple angles. Butler automation: No-code automations with 200+ recipes handle repetitive actions automatically. Workspace views: Cross-board rollups provide program-level visibility across multiple projects. Pricing Free: $0 (up to 10 collaborators, 10 open boards) Standard: $5/user/month (billed annually) Premium: $10/user/month (billed annually) Enterprise: $17.50/user/month (billed annually) Considerations The free plan ’’ s limits on collaborators and boards can be restrictive for growing teams. Performance issues may arise when boards become overloaded with thousands of cards. 5. Jira Synonymous with agile development, Jira remains the standard for technical teams. It bridges the gap between code and company strategy, allowing organizations to manage software development alongside broader business operations. With a massive footprint in the DevOps space, it connects engineering workflows with the rest of the enterprise. For teams evaluating alternatives, here’s a guide to Jira alternatives for small teams . Rovo AI agents automate routine processes and interpret natural language queries, while flexible workflow customization lets teams switch between Scrum and Kanban as needed. The free plan supports up to 10 users, making it accessible for small engineering teams getting started. Best for : Software development and engineering teams managing agile workflows, sprint planning, and issue tracking at scale . Key features Agile-native boards: Scrum and Kanban boards, velocity tracking, and sprint planning to keep development cycles moving. Rovo AI agents: Automate routine processes and interpret natural language queries to accelerate responses. Deep DevOps integration: Native connections to Bitbucket, GitHub, and CI/CD pipelines keep engineering workflows connected. Pricing Free: Up to 10 users Standard: $7.91/user/month (billed annually) Premium: $14.54/user/month (billed annually) Enterprise: Custom pricing Considerations Full AI capabilities and advanced features are gated behind higher tiers. Non-technical teams often find the interface unintuitive without dedicated onboarding. 6. Wrike Security and deep governance sit at the core of Wrike ‘s offering. Designed for the enterprise, it excels in managing complex project hierarchies and facilitating cross-functional collaboration. It is a strong fit for organizations with formal PMOs and strict compliance mandates. Wrike covers the full project lifecycle from intake and approvals to proofing and analytics. SOC 2 Type II, ISO certifications, Wrike Lock (customer-managed encryption), and data residency options provide the security foundation that regulated industries require. Best for: Mid-to-large enterprises looking for feature-rich resource allocation, detailed approval workflows, and governance across multiple departments. Key features Resource optimization: Capacity planning, job roles, and utilization tracking help managers balance workloads across teams. Enterprise security: SOC 2 Type II, ISO certifications, Wrike Lock, and data residency meet the requirements of regulated industries. Full lifecycle management: Covers everything from intake and approvals to proofing and analytics in a single workspace. Pricing Free: Basic workflow management Team: $10/user/month (2-15 users) Business: $25/user/month (5-200 users) Enterprise and Pinnacle: Custom pricing Considerations The platform’s depth results in a steeper learning curve than simpler alternatives. Pricing can be complex, with high-end features and add-ons increasing the total cost of ownership. 7. Zoho Projects If your organization already relies on the Zoho ecosystem, Zoho Projects is the logical next step. It integrates deeply with Zoho CRM, Books, and other suite apps, offering an end-to-end system that handles everything from planning to billing. It also supports hybrid delivery methods, accommodating both traditional and agile workflows via its Sprints integration. Advanced planning features include critical path analysis, baselines, and earned value management (EVM). Built-in time tracking and direct invoicing through Zoho Books make it particularly useful for services teams tracking billable hours. Best for: Businesses that want to consolidate their operations — time tracking, budgeting, and invoicing — within the Zoho suite. Key features Methodology flexibility: Switch between Gantt charts and Scrum boards via Zoho Sprints integration to match your team’s delivery approach. Deep planning capabilities: Critical path analysis, baselines, and earned value management give project managers granular control. Operational integration: Built-in time tracking, issue tracking with SLAs, and direct invoicing through Zoho Books keep everything connected. Pricing Free: Up to 5 users Premium: Competitive per-user pricing Enterprise: Portfolio dashboards and global custom modules Projects Plus bundle: $16/user/month (includes Projects, Sprints, Analytics, WorkDrive) Considerations Advanced configurations can be complex, requiring a dedicated learning period for administrators. The mobile app offers limited functionality for deep administrative work compared to the web version. 8. Hive Hive integrates native chat, email, and proofing directly into the workflow, making it a strong candidate for creative agencies and marketing teams that need to handle approvals and communication without switching apps. Features are often developed based on user requests, giving the platform a community-driven development cycle. Buzz AI helps teams draft content and automate repetitive workflows without technical expertise. Gantt, Kanban, calendar, and table views all support intuitive drag-and-drop functionality for flexible work visualization. Best for: Creative and marketing teams that want to house communication, project execution, and creative proofing in one place. Key features Integrated communication: Native chat, Hive Mail, and markup features are designed specifically for reviewing and approving creative assets. Buzz AI: Draft content and automate repetitive workflows without requiring technical expertise. Flexible views: Gantt, Kanban, calendar, and table formats all support drag-and-drop for intuitive work organization. Pricing Free: Up to 10 members Starter: $5/user/month (billed annually) Teams: $12/user/month (billed annually) Enterprise: Custom pricing Considerations Key features like proofing and resourcing are paid add-ons, increasing costs beyond the base price. Some users report a learning curve and mobile usability limitations for complex project work. 9. Bitrix24 Small to mid-sized businesses looking for a “business in a box” often turn to Bitrix24. It combines project management with CRM, video conferencing, and document handling in a single environment. The platform ’’ s flat-rate pricing model offers predictability for organizations that want to avoid per-user fees while consolidating their software stack. AI CoPilot helps teams generate descriptions, create checklists, and produce project summaries automatically. Teams can switch between Kanban, Gantt, Scrum, and workload planning views to match their preferred way of working. Best for: Companies seeking to unify CRM, projects, and communication in a single environment with predictable monthly costs . Key features All-in-one workspace: Merges workflows, CRM, chat, video calls, and docs into a single unified environment, eliminating the need to juggle multiple subscriptions. Project visualization: Kanban, Gantt, Scrum, and workload planning views accommodate different team preferences. AI CoPilot: Generates descriptions, checklists, and project summaries automatically to reduce manual work. Pricing Free: Unlimited users (basic features) Basic: $61/month (5 users) Standard: $124/month (50 users) Professional: $249/month (100 users) Enterprise: $499+/month (250+ users) Considerations The interface can feel complex due to the sheer number of features bundled into the platform. Live chat support is restricted to paid plans, which limits help for free-tier users. 10. Nifty Nifty unifies project tracking with team chat and milestone management, keeping everyone focused on the roadmap. It is particularly useful for client-facing teams and agencies that need to keep stakeholders updated automatically as work progresses toward key milestones. Milestones update automatically as linked items are completed, giving stakeholders real-time visibility without manual reporting. Discussions are threaded directly into project workspaces, keeping conversations in context rather than scattered across email and chat apps. Best for : Teams that want milestone-based organization where progress is automatically tracked and communication happens in context . Key features Automated roadmaps: Milestones update automatically as linked workflows are completed, keeping stakeholders informed in real time. Contextual communication: Discussions are threaded directly into project workspaces, reducing context switching. Varied views: Kanban, timeline, swimlane, and calendar views let teams organize work in their preferred format. Pricing Free: $0 (2 projects) Personal: $7/member/month (40 projects) Business: $16/member/month (unlimited projects) Enterprise: Custom pricing Considerations Some users have reported occasional bugs and interface glitches during peak usage. The platform may lack the depth required for rapidly scaling enterprises compared to more established players. How to choose the right project management app With dozens of options, how do you cut through the noise? The best project management app isn ’’ t the one with the longest feature list — it’. A five-person startup doesn’t need the same permission controls as a 5,000-person organization. A platform with native AI assistants, agents, and automations will deliver faster time-to-value than one requiring third-party add-ons. title: What is a Sales Kickoff (SKO)? Complete Guide for 2026
body_text: What is the Annual Sales Kickoff? The annual sales kickoff is the yearly gathering of a company's sales force. It's typically held at the start of the fiscal year, the golden time for change and transformation. It's usually the most comprehensive sales team event, and it covers: ‍ Share success stories Celebrations of the previous year's achievements; Strategies for the year ahead; Product launches; Team-building initiatives ; Important announcements; ‍ While some companies also hold quarterly sales rallies for alignment, the annual SKO is the flagship event. Here, sales organizations also set the tone for the coming year . It's often the only time the entire sales team gathers in person and an opportunity for strengthening relationships and company culture. ‍ Why Host a Sales Kickoff Event? Over 50% of sales teams with structured kickoff events see better communication, collaboration, stronger pipeline growth, and improved forecast accuracy. The ROI comes from multiple angles that compound over time: ‍ Builds Bridges & Boosts Engagement: A sales kickoff energizes team building and strengthens company culture, driving employee engagement throughout the year. Empowers Through Unified Training: SKO training sessions enable sales professionals to work smarter, accelerate skill development, and translate learning into real performance improvements. Sets the Course for Success: Thoughtfully planned sales events and sales teams corporate retreats help teams clarify business goals and objectives, align around the event’s agenda, and focus on measurable success metrics. Connects Teams in Real Time, Anywhere: Technology integration through virtual sales kickoff events ensures every employee stays connected and engaged, no matter where they are. Leads with Vision: Visible executive leadership at SKOs models strong management, drives team dynamics, and inspires the entire team to overcome challenges together. Networking That Fuels Collaboration: SKO networking builds relationships and improves communication for collaborative problem-solving throughout the sales cycle. ‍ How to Run a Sales Kickoff Meeting or Event For a successful sales kickoff to happen, the following framework plays a crucial role. ‍ 1. Set Clear Objectives Define specific and measurable goals, like “Reach 75% adoption of the new process within 30 days.” Every part of your sales kickoff agenda must connect to these objectives in order to reach real results. ‍ 2. Choose Your Format Decide between in-person, virtual, or hybrid based on budget, team distribution, and goals: ‍ In-person events deliver unmatched relationship building, but cost significantly more Virtual sales kickoffs save money and include remote team member,s but require more effort to maintain engagement Hybrid approaches try to capture both benefits ‍ 3. Build an Engaging Agenda Balance business content with connection: ‍ Mornings: Sales strategy and product training Afternoons: Interactive sessions and team-building activities that reinforce sales skills ‍ Remember to include: ‍ Mix formats (keynote speakers, breakout sessions , role-playing, panels) Use storytelling and success stories rather than just data ‍ 4. Include Essential Elements Don't forget to include the following: ‍ Leadership presentations on company vision and priorities Product training with hands-on practice Sales process updates with interactive learning Recognition and awards ceremony for top performers Time for networking ‍ 5. Measure Impact Immediate feedback through end-of-day surveys Knowledge retention tests 1-2 weeks later Behavioral change tracking over the following months ‍ Sales professionals are results-oriented, so if they don't see clear value, engagement drops fast. ‍ How Long Should a Sales Kickoff Be? The optimal length depends on your objectives and format: ‍ Traditional Annual Sales Kickoff: 2-4 Days Most companies run in-person events over 2-3 full days , often with travel days on either end. This allows enough time for comprehensive content without overwhelming participants. Four-day events are becoming less common as attention spans shrink and people resist being away from home that long. Single-day events rarely provide enough time for training and relationship building. ‍ Quarterly Sales Rallies: 1-2 Days More companies are shifting to shorter, more frequent touchpoints. These work well as virtual sales kickoffs or regional gatherings. ‍ Hybrid/Split: Training Sessions and Sales Strategy in Two Formats Some sales organizations spread content across weeks. For example, weekly virtual training sessions for a month, culminating in a 1-2 day in-person celebration and team-building event . This approach improves retention and keeps the single gathering manageable. ‍ Rule of Thumb Keep your sales kickoff agenda balanced. Avoid more than 6–8 hours of presentations per day to maintain engagement. Instead, spread content over multiple days or assign some as pre-work or post-event resources. Consider your team’s needs: field reps may need more time for team-building to boost morale , while inside sales might focus more on training. ‍ What Activities Should Be Included? Aiming for a successful sales kickoff event? Combine business content with engagement activities: ‍ Essential Business Activities Leadership Presentations: Executives share the company vision and priorities, linking sales goals to overall objectives. Give financial updates, but also keep it inspiring. Product Training: Hands-on sessions with role-playing and real Q&A ensure reps understand new features and can handle them confidently. Sales Process Workshops: Interactive workshops help practice new methodologies, like qualification frameworks or negotiation tactics. Breakout Sessions: Smaller groups focus on specific roles, allowing deeper discussions and active participation. Success Stories: Top performers share tactics and case studies that the whole team can learn from and remember. Executive Q&A: Open forums with leadership build trust, allow tough questions, and address concerns early. ‍ Team-Building Activities Recognition and awards ceremony celebrate achievements from the previous year. Public recognition of top employees sets standards and motivates the broader team. Social meals and other one-day retreat ideas create the informal connections that enable future collaboration. Don't overschedule and leave space for organic conversation. Competitions and team games that reinforce sales skills (negotiation exercises, pitch competitions, problem-solving challenges) combine fun with learning. Outdoor activities can break up intensive content days. These work best when they subtly reinforce teamwork or resilience rather than feeling disconnected from work. Volunteer or charity activities where the team gives back together can build culture while serving a higher purpose. ‍ The Mix Aim for roughly 60-70% business content and 30-40% team building and networking . Too much business burns people out. Too little makes it feel like the company is avoiding real priorities. ‍ Measuring SKO Success Beyond Sales Goals Measuring overall success requires tracking multiple dimensions across different timeframes: ‍ Immediate Metrics (During/Right After the Event) Track attendance , session engagement , and social interaction . Use real-time surveys to measure relevance, immediate takeaways, and likelihood to recommend. ‍ Real-time feedback scores from end-of-day surveys while experiences are fresh: ‍ How relevant was each session? (1-5 scale) What will you apply immediately? What needs more depth? How likely are you to recommend this event format for next year? ‍ Social engagement and networking. At in-person events, observe whether people are connecting during social time. For virtual sales kickoffs, track chat participation and breakout room engagement. ‍ Short-Term Metrics (Weeks 1-4) Test knowledge retention and tool/process adoption . Sales managers check if teams apply new skills in real situations. Quiz reps two weeks later to see what stuck. Low scores mean your training approach needs adjustment. Within 30 days , what percentage of the sales team is actually using the new CRM features or following the updated qualification methodology? Promote manager check-ins where sales managers assess whether their teams are applying learnings. ‍ Medium-Term Metrics (Months 2-6) Behavioral change in key activities you aimed to influence: Are sales reps using the discovery framework? Are they positioning products differently? Are they collaborating more effectively with customer success teams? Pipeline quality improvements. Are deals moving faster through stages? Are win rates improving in specific deal types? Adoption sustainability. Initial enthusiasm fades. Track whether behaviors from the sales kickoff meeting are still present months later or if old habits have returned. ‍ Long-Term Metrics (Months 6-12) Quota attainment. Is the sales team hitting the objectives established at the kickoff event? Compare performance to previous periods. Revenue impact. Did the entire sales force contribute to growth? Are specific initiatives (new product lines, new market segments) gaining traction? Retention and satisfaction. Are sales reps staying with the company? The Aberdeen Group research states that companies investing in comprehensive sales training experience up to 53% lower turnover . Team performance culture. Are success stories being shared? Are top performers mentoring others? Has collaboration improved? These softer measures indicate if the event created culture shifts. ‍ Sales Kickoff Trends to Watch for in 2025 The sales kickoff landscape continues to shift. What worked five years ago might feel dated today. Here are the top sales kickoff trends by forward-thinking sales leaders: ‍ 1. Virtual and Hybrid Events Become Sophisticated Virtual sales kickoffs have advanced beyond video calls to immersive, engaging experiences: ‍ Virtual venues with gamified learning and digital breakout rooms Hybrid split: virtual for training-heavy quarterly events, in-person for annual culture-building Technologies: interactive polling/Q&A, breakout sessions, gamification, on-demand libraries ‍ 2. AI and Technology Integration AI-powered tools are central to SKOs for consistent technology adoption: ‍ Conversation intelligence platforms for call analysis Predictive analytics for pipeline and deal scoring Automated prospecting tools AI-driven virtual role-play simulations with real-time coaching and troubleshooting ‍ The sales kickoff meeting becomes the moment to train everyone on these technologies together, ensuring consistent adoption. ‍ 3. Personalization at Scale Customized experiences replace one-size-fits-all agendas: ‍ Role-based tracks: onboarding for new reps, advanced tactics for veterans Learning paths focused on individual skill gaps Territory/vertical-specific sales strategy sessions Individual goal-setting workshops linking personal ambition to company goals ‍ This makes the entire event feel designed for each person specifically, instead of delivered generically. ‍ 4. Wellness and Mental Health Focus Wellness and mental health are also team-building trends for 2025 . And let's face it: sales is high-pressure work. The worry is constant. Progressive sales kickoff agendas now acknowledge this reality: ‍ Stress management and work-life balance sessions Mental health activities Open promotion of mental health resources and peer support Burnout prevention strategies for managers Executive-led discussions demonstrating organizational commitment ‍ Sales leaders realize that team morale and mental health directly impact performance, retention, and the success of the organization. ‍ 5. Sustainability Initiatives Companies are reducing the carbon footprint of sales kickoff events without sacrificing impact: ‍ Eco-friendly venue choices that prioritize renewable energy and waste reduction programs. Digital-first approaches replace printed materials with mobile apps and digital workbooks. Local and regional formats reduce travel by hosting multiple smaller events rather than flying everyone to headquarters. Carbon offset programs for necessary travel acknowledge the environmental cost and invest in reduction projects. Sustainable catering sources locally, reduces meat-heavy menus, and eliminates single-use items. Many sales teams are questioning whether every event needs to be in-person, or if virtual sales kickoffs can deliver value with less environmental impact. The answer for most: hybrid approaches that save in-person for moments that truly require face-to-face connection. ‍ How Much Does a Sales Kickoff Cost? Costs vary significantly based on format, scale, and location: ‍ Virtual Sales Kickoffs: $5,000-$50,000 Platform fees for specialized event software Production costs (video, graphics, technical support) Digital content creation Virtual activities and entertainment Keynote speakers (often lower fees for virtual) ‍ In-Person Events: $100,000-$1,000,000+ Venue rental and meeting spaces Travel and accommodation for all sales team members Catering (breakfast, lunch, dinner, breaks) Audio/visual production Keynote speakers and entertainment Team-building activities Event staff and coordination Printed materials and swag ‍ Per-Person Budgets Virtual: $50-$200 per attendee In-person: $1,500-$3,000 per attendee (all-in with travel) ‍ Cost-Saving Strategies Choose shoulder season dates for better venue rates Select locations outside major expensive cities Go hybrid Use internal subject matter experts instead of expensive external keynote speakers Negotiate venue packages that bundle accommodation with meeting space Partner with vendors who might sponsor portions in exchange for product showcase time ‍ The key is aligning spend with objectives. If relationship building is the priority, cutting in-person elements to save money undermines the goal. If training is primary, virtual might deliver better ROI by allowing frequent touchpoints throughout the year. ‍ Ready to Plan Your Next Retreat? Whether you're organizing a large-scale sales kickoff meeting or an intimate sales team offsite , partnering with the right expert can transform your event’s success. At TeamOut , we’ve led over 1,500 retreats , with access to more than 4,000 vetted venues worldwide , helping sales leaders save an average of 30% on venue costs with transparent quotes delivered in 24 hours. ‍ From sourcing venues to full-service retreat planning, including logistics and on-site support, we handle every detail. This allows sales managers and sales reps to focus on the sales kickoff agenda aligned with the company’s goals. ‍ With a satisfaction rate of 95% , our approach ensures the entire team stays inspired and connected. Our tailored sales kickoff meeting ideas boost team morale, foster healthy competition, and promote personal growth. By integrating product teams and encouraging the sharing of success stories, sales objectives become clear, and success becomes the driver of the year ahead. ‍ Let's talk about your next sales kickoff. Schedule a free call with us today . Together, we help plan the event that aligns with your company's objectives and sets your sales team up for an outstanding year. ‍
